Neonates of the Antarctic starry skate emerge from their egg cases with a total length of 18 cm [Lb = 18 cm], a dimension consistent with the modest body size of newborn elasmobranchs inhabiting high-latitude shelf environments. This birth length is derived from observed pup lengths of 10 to 12 cm, which increase slightly upon full expansion after hatching. Under the persistently cold conditions of the Southern Ocean, where bottom temperatures hover around 4 °C [T = 4 °C], the incubating embryo develops slowly, and the total duration from oviposition to hatching spans approximately 290 days [ab = approximately 290 days]. This protracted embryonic period stands in marked contrast to the faster developmental schedules documented in temperate skate species and likely reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by near-freezing waters. Yolk absorption proceeds gradually, sustaining the embryo through months of organogenesis until the young skate is fully formed and capable of independent locomotion at the moment of emergence from the egg case. Newly hatched individuals immediately assume a demersal existence, foraging on small benthic invertebrates in the same habitat occupied by the adults.

Female Amblyraja georgiana achieve an ultimate total length of 115 cm [Li = 115 cm], making this species one of the larger rajid skates found in subantarctic waters. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a steep allometric curve, such that a female at her asymptotic size attains an ultimate wet weight of 16,200 grams [Wwi = 16,200 grams]. This heavy body mass reflects a robust skeletal structure and thick musculature, which are typical of bottom-dwelling elasmobranchs that rely on powerful pectoral fins for propulsion across the seafloor. In comparison to other members of the genus Amblyraja, the maximum size recorded for A. georgiana sits near the upper end of the size spectrum; only the closely related Amblyraja radiata reaches comparable dimensions in North Atlantic waters. Field surveys suggest that females continue growing slowly throughout most of their adult lives, with growth increments becoming increasingly negligible as they approach the apparent upper bound imposed by the allometric constraint linking body length to wet weight. No male individuals of similarly large proportions have been documented, indicating pronounced sexual dimorphism in ultimate size for this species.

The onset of reproductive maturity in females is marked by the attainment of a total length at puberty of 85 cm [Lp = 85 cm], a size typically achieved when the animal reaches approximately 80 to 90 cm in total length. At this threshold, ovarian follicles begin to enlarge and the reproductive tract develops the capacity to support gestation and subsequent oviposition. Under the stable thermal regime of the Southern Ocean, with ambient water temperatures near 4 °C [T = 4 °C], the full lifespan of the Antarctic starry skate extends to approximately 14 years [am = approximately 14 years]. This longevity is considerable for a skate of its body size and aligns with the general life-history pattern observed in other cold-water elasmobranchs, which tend to exhibit slower growth rates and extended lifespans relative to their temperate counterparts. The combination of a late maturation age and a long adult phase suggests that A. georgiana invests heavily in somatic persistence before channelling resources into annual reproductive bouts. Individuals that survive the vulnerable juvenile period therefore enjoy a lengthy reproductive window during which they can produce multiple egg cases over successive breeding seasons.

The maximum reproductive rate of female Amblyraja georgiana is constrained by the low metabolic rates typical of polar ectotherms. Under conditions providing a stable ambient temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C], available data indicate that a female can deposit approximately 36 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 36 eggs per year], which corresponds to roughly three eggs laid each month. This egg production rate is derived from an analysis of ovarian fecundity and observed egg-case deposition frequencies in captive individuals maintained at controlled temperatures. The resulting annual egg output is equivalent to slightly more than 0.7 eggs per week across the calendar year, a modest figure when compared to the fecundity of many temperate skate species that may produce multiple egg cases per week during the peak of their breeding season. Each egg case contains a single fertilised ovum encased in a tough, collagenous capsule that provides mechanical protection and a stable microenvironment for the developing embryo. The deposition of these capsules continues throughout the year under laboratory conditions, suggesting that the species does not exhibit a sharply defined annual breeding season in its native habitat.

Field observations and physiological data further illuminate the demographic strategy of this skate. The mean age at birth, representing the interval between oviposition and hatching, was quantified at approximately 9.5 months [ab = approximately 9.5 months] when referring to calendar months at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. In terms of longevity, the oldest documented individuals in mark-recapture programmes have achieved an approximate age of 14 years [am = 14 years], confirming that this species is among the longer-lived skates in the Southern Ocean fauna at a temperature of 4 °C [T = 4 °C]. Calibration of growth models using vertebral band counts has independently validated this lifespan estimate. The combination of a delayed maturation schedule, low annual fecundity, and extended adult lifespan positions the Antarctic starry skate with life-history traits finely tuned to the stable but energetically challenging conditions of its high-latitude marine environment.
